editorialDrafts.en: The Sunday after Easter is called in albis, recalling the white baptismal garments worn by the neophytes during Easter week. In ancient Rome, the laying aside of these garments was associated with the vigil at the Lateran, while the Sunday observance came to be linked with Saint Pancras, the young martyr whose fidelity recalled the promises of baptism. The liturgical readings invite the newly baptised—and all the faithful—to profess belief in the risen Christ, as Saint Thomas does in the Gospel. These historical customs help explain the day; they are not ceremonies to be added to the 1962 Mass.
editorialDrafts.fr: Le dimanche après Pâques est appelé in albis, en souvenir des vêtements blancs portés par les néophytes durant l’octave pascale. Dans la Rome ancienne, leur déposition était liée à la vigile au Latran, tandis que la célébration dominicale fut associée à Saint-Pancrace, jeune martyr dont la fidélité rappelait les promesses du baptême. Les lectures invitent les nouveaux baptisés, comme tous les fidèles, à croire au Christ ressuscité et à professer cette foi avec saint Thomas dans l’Évangile. Ces usages historiques éclairent le sens du jour : ils ne sont pas des cérémonies à ajouter à la Messe de 1962.
editorialDrafts.verification: ICRSP article verified directly. The Holy See's Pontifical Academy Cultorum Martyrum distinguishes the Lateran vigil deposition of white baptismal clothing from the later Sunday Pancras observance and renewal of baptismal promises. Historical scope corrected in both drafts. Exact calendar owner ID, final 1962 Proper comparison, editorial theological sign-off and reproduction-rights status remain unapproved.

independentEvidence.finding: Pontifical Academy Cultorum Martyrum distinguishes white-robe deposition at the Lateran vigil from a later Sunday ceremony at San Pancrazio including baptismal promises; do not collapse the two into one Mass ritual.

Traditional Missal-form summary identifies Dominica in Albis as a first-class Sunday with station at St Pancras and Quasi modo as the Introit; this is a secondary witness, not canonical resolver certification.
Original source page contains commentary on Dominica in Albis, neophyte white garments and the St Pancras station, but its hosted translation is not adopted.

editorialDrafts.en: The Mass of the Sacred Heart has not always used the same formulary. The devotion entered the universal Roman calendar in the nineteenth century, while a substantially revised Mass and Office were introduced under Pius XI in 1929. Earlier commentaries therefore sometimes explain prayers that are not those of the 1962 Missal. For the Mass actually celebrated, the approved Proper of the selected date remains the reference.
editorialDrafts.fr: La fête du Sacré-Cœur n'a pas toujours possédé le même formulaire. Son inscription au calendrier romain universel remonte au XIXᵉ siècle, tandis qu'une Messe et un Office largement remaniés furent introduits sous Pie XI en 1929. Les commentaires anciens expliquent donc parfois des prières différentes de celles du Missel de 1962. Pour la célébration effective, il faut se référer au propre approuvé du jour choisi.
editorialDrafts.verification: Pius XI 1928 document and independent historical study corroborate chronological distinction. Still require 1929 SCR decree or verified print witness, canonical 1962 Proper ID, owner comparison and editorial sign-off; no historic alternate Proper import.

independentEvidence.finding: Pius XI explicitly orders the feast raised to first class with octave and annual reparation prayer, in his 8 May 1928 encyclical.
ICRSP states an earlier 1856 universal feast formulary was superseded by a second Mass and Office promulgated under Pius XI in 1929; original decree not yet collated.
Independent liturgical-historical study dates the new Mass/Office to the Sacred Congregation of Rites of 29 January 1929 and earlier universal recognition to 23 August 1856.
